## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- **Explain** the **curse of dimensionality** and dimensionality reduction by **projection**: real
  data lies near a low-dimensional subspace, so axes carrying little variance can be dropped.
  *(Understand)*
- **Explain** PCA -- it finds orthogonal **principal components** (the axes of maximum variance, via
  the **SVD** of the centered data), ordered by the variance they capture. *(Understand)*
- **Apply** `PCA` with scikit-learn: `fit_transform` to project, `explained_variance_ratio_` to read
  variance, and `n_components` to keep a target fraction (95% -> 28 of 64 on the digits). *(Apply)*
- **Analyze** the compression trade-off -- a classifier on 28 components nearly matches all 64 (0.954
  vs 0.957), and **reconstruction** error falls as `d` grows. *(Analyze)*
- **Relate** PCA to an autoencoder (PCA = a linear autoencoder: project = encode, reconstruct =
  decode) and read its mechanism as the SVD of the centered matrix. *(Understand / Analyze)*

## Why This Matters

A handwritten-digit image in the lab is 64 numbers -- an 8x8 grid of pixels. But you do not need all
64 to tell a 3 from an 8: the border pixels are almost always blank, and neighbouring pixels move
together. Most of those 64 dimensions are nearly redundant.

That redundancy is the rule, not the exception, and it matters because high-dimensional space is
mostly **empty**. As you add features, points spread out exponentially, every point becomes far from
every other, models overfit, and training slows -- the **curse of dimensionality**. The escape is that
real data almost always lies near a much lower-dimensional **subspace**. **Principal Component
Analysis** finds that subspace -- the handful of directions along which the data actually varies -- and
projects onto it. On the digits, 2 of the 64 axes already separate the classes by eye, and 28 capture
95% of everything, with a classifier on those 28 nearly as accurate as on all 64.

::: {.callout-tip title="Analogy"}
Photographing a crowd, you instinctively stand where the people are most **spread out** -- a side angle
where everyone is visible, not an end-on view where they hide behind each other. PCA picks that angle
automatically: its first principal component is the direction of greatest spread (variance), the
second is the best remaining direction at right angles to it, and so on. Keep the first few angles and
you have a flat photo that still tells the crowd apart; throw away the rest and you lose almost
nothing, because along those directions everyone already looked the same.
:::

## The Curse of Dimensionality

Add dimensions and intuition breaks. In high-D space, randomly scattered points are almost all far
apart and near the edges of the region they occupy, so any new point sits far from your training data
-- a prediction becomes a long extrapolation, and the model is more likely to overfit. Reaching a fixed
data density needs exponentially more samples as dimensions grow, which is hopeless in practice.

The saving grace is the **manifold assumption**: real high-dimensional datasets tend to lie close to a
much lower-dimensional surface inside that space. Digit images do not fill all of 64-D pixel space --
they cluster on a thin sheet of "things that look like digits." **Dimensionality reduction** finds a
low-dimensional representation; the simplest kind is a **projection** onto a flat subspace, and PCA
chooses the best flat subspace there is.

## Principal Component Analysis

PCA identifies the axis along which the data has the **largest variance**, then the axis orthogonal to
it with the largest *remaining* variance, and so on -- one **principal component** per original
dimension, ordered by variance captured. To reduce to `d` dimensions, keep the first `d` components
and **project** the (centered) data onto them:

$$
\mathbf{X}_{d} = \mathbf{X}_c \, \mathbf{W}_d
$$

where $\mathbf{X}_c$ is the mean-centered data and $\mathbf{W}_d$ holds the first `d` components as its
columns. The components come from the **singular value decomposition** of the centered matrix:

$$
\mathbf{X}_c = \mathbf{U}\,\mathbf{\Sigma}\,\mathbf{V}^{\top}, \qquad
\text{principal components} = \text{rows of } \mathbf{V}^{\top}
$$

and each component's variance is its squared singular value over $m-1$. (scikit-learn centers the data
for you; you do not center it yourself.)

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A["Center the data<br/>(subtract the mean)"] --> B["SVD of the centered matrix:<br/>orthogonal axes of max variance"]
  B --> C["Order components<br/>by variance captured"]
  C --> D["Keep the top d<br/>(e.g. 95% of variance)"]
  D --> E["Project the data<br/>onto those d axes"]
```

`explained_variance_ratio_` reports the fraction of total variance each component holds. On the lab's
digits the first two components hold 0.146 and 0.137 -- together 28% of everything in just 2 of 64
axes, enough to plot the classes and see them separate.

## Choosing the Number of Components

For visualization you take 2 or 3 components. For compression, instead of guessing, pick the number
that preserves a target fraction of the variance. Take the **cumulative** sum of
`explained_variance_ratio_` and find where it crosses, say, 0.95:

| Variance kept | Components (of 64) |
|---------------|-------------------:|
| 80% | 13 |
| 90% | 21 |
| **95%** | **28** |
| 99% | 41 |

So 95% of the digits' variance survives in **28** of the 64 dimensions. You can read this off the
cumulative curve, or just pass the fraction directly: `PCA(n_components=0.95)` returns 28 components.
The diminishing return is visible in the table -- the first 13 components buy 80%, but the last 4% of
variance (95% -> 99%) costs another 13, because the tail components each carry almost nothing.

## Reconstruction and the Compression Trade-off

A projection is **lossy**: `inverse_transform` maps the `d`-dimensional code back to the original
space, but it returns an approximation. The reconstruction error measures the loss, and it falls as
`d` grows -- 13.4 (MSE) at 2 components, 0.935 at 28, exactly 0 at the full 64. The reconstructed
digits at 28 components are visibly the same numbers, only smoothed.

What you keep is the **predictive signal**. In the lab a logistic-regression classifier scores 0.957
on all 64 raw features and **0.954** on the 28 PCA components -- a 0.003 drop for less than half the
dimensions -- and the accuracy-vs-components curve (0.600 at 2, 0.924 at 10, 0.954 at 28) shows the
signal concentrates in the first couple dozen components. Fewer features also means a smaller, faster
model, less prone to overfitting. That is why PCA is a standard **preprocessing** step, not just a
plotting trick.

::: {.callout-note title="Deep Dive: PCA is a linear autoencoder (Optional)" collapse="true"}

`L20 — Autoencoders` introduced a network that compresses its input through a narrow bottleneck and
reconstructs it, and named PCA as its linear cousin. Now the loop closes. PCA *is* an autoencoder
whose encoder and decoder are both **linear**:

- **Encode:** project onto the components, $\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{X}_c \mathbf{W}_d$ (the bottleneck is
  the `d`-dimensional code).
- **Decode:** reconstruct, $\hat{\mathbf{X}} = \mathbf{z}\,\mathbf{W}_d^{\top}$ (plus the mean).

Minimizing the reconstruction error over all *linear* encoders/decoders gives exactly the top `d`
principal components. An autoencoder generalizes this by letting the encoder and decoder be nonlinear
networks, so it can bend around curved (manifold) structure that PCA's straight-line projection
misses -- at the cost of training a network instead of taking one SVD. PCA is the fast, closed-form,
linear special case.
:::

## When to Use PCA

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  S{"Why reduce<br/>the dimensions?"}
  S -- "plot high-D data" --> V["PCA to 2-3 components<br/>(visualization)"]
  S -- "speed up / regularize<br/>a downstream model" --> C["PCA keeping 95-99%<br/>of the variance"]
  S -- "the structure is a curved,<br/>twisted manifold" --> M["nonlinear methods:<br/>t-SNE, LLE (L27)"]
```

PCA is the first thing to reach for: it is fast (a single SVD), closed-form, and interpretable. Its
limits set up the rest of Unit VII -- it is **linear**, so it cannot unroll a curved manifold (that is
t-SNE and LLE, L27), and it assumes the directions of **most variance are the most useful**, which is
not always true (a tiny-variance direction can carry the label).

## Common Pitfalls

- **Forgetting to scale features on different units.** PCA chases variance, so a feature measured in
  large units (grams vs kilograms) dominates the components purely because its numbers are bigger.
  Standardize first when scales differ. (The digits are all 0-16, so the lab does not scale them.)
- **Assuming variance equals signal.** PCA keeps the highest-variance directions, but the class
  information can live in a low-variance direction it discards. Variance is a useful default, not a
  guarantee.
- **Treating reconstruction as lossless.** Any `d < n` loses information; check the reconstruction
  error or the explained-variance ratio to know how much.
- **Expecting PCA to unroll a curved manifold.** PCA is a *linear* projection -- it cannot follow a
  Swiss-roll twist. Use a manifold method (t-SNE, LLE -- L27) for that.
- **Running PCA on data you forgot to center.** scikit-learn centers for you, but a hand-rolled SVD
  must subtract the mean first, or the first component just points at the mean.

## FAQ / Industry Reality

**"How many components should I keep?"** -- For a plot, 2 or 3. For preprocessing, keep a variance
target (95-99%) with `PCA(n_components=0.95)`, or treat `n_components` as a hyperparameter and tune it
by cross-validation against your downstream model.

**"Do I scale before PCA?"** -- If your features are on different units or ranges, yes -- standardize
first, or the largest-numbered feature hijacks the components. If they share a scale (like pixel
intensities), centering (which PCA does for you) is enough.

**"What is randomized PCA?"** -- `svd_solver="randomized"` approximates the top `d` components with a
stochastic algorithm that is far faster than a full SVD when `d` is much smaller than the number of
features. scikit-learn picks it automatically on large data; same result, less time.

**"When is PCA the wrong tool?"** -- When the structure is nonlinear (a curved manifold) -- use t-SNE
or LLE (L27) -- or when the useful signal sits in a low-variance direction PCA would drop.

## Summary / Cheat-sheet

| Concept | The one-liner |
|---------|---------------|
| Curse of dimensionality | high-D space is sparse -> overfitting, slow training; reduce dimensions |
| PCA | project onto the orthogonal axes of maximum variance (the principal components) |
| Mechanism | the SVD of the centered data; components = rows of V^T, variance = singular value^2/(m-1) |
| `explained_variance_ratio_` | fraction of total variance each component holds |
| Choosing d | cumulative variance to a target: 95% -> 28 of 64 (or `PCA(n_components=0.95)`) |
| Compression payoff | classifier 0.954 (28 comps) vs 0.957 (64) -- nearly free, smaller + faster |
| Reconstruction | `inverse_transform`; lossy, MSE falls with d (13.4 -> 0.935 -> 0) |
| PCA vs autoencoder | PCA = linear autoencoder; an autoencoder is the nonlinear generalization |
| Limits | linear (no curved manifolds -> t-SNE/LLE, L27); assumes variance = signal; scale first |
